opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the most underrated parts of the whole pipeline. When people think about pre-training, they mostly think about scale: more tokens, more compute. But the quality of those tokens matters enormously, and the web is incredibly noisy. Spam, boilerplate, SEO junk, near-duplicates, broken text.

Historically you'd filter with heuristics, like perplexity thresholds, or small classifiers trained to look like Wikipedia. Those help, but they're fairly crude. What's exciting now is that the previous generation of Llama is good enough to judge the data for the next generation. You can ask it whether a document is informative, whether it teaches something, whether it has reasoning or code or math worth learning from. And it makes those calls with a nuance that simple heuristics just don't have.

In practice you can't run a big model over trillions of tokens, so you use it to label a sample and then distill that judgment into a smaller, cheaper classifier that runs at web scale. But the signal starts with Llama.

The other thing I find valuable is control. Once you have a model that understands content, you can classify by topic, domain, difficulty, or language, not just good versus bad. That lets you shape the data mix deliberately: upweight code and math, rebalance domains, find underrepresented areas. That has a real effect on downstream capabilities, especially reasoning.

There's also a nice flywheel. Each Llama generation gets better partly because of better data, and then that better model becomes a better annotator and filter for the next one. That's a big part of how I see progress compounding, not just through architecture or scale, but through models helping curate their own training data.

r001.rationale: The response says Llama can classify by topic and domain, letting teams deliberately shape the data mix by rebalancing domains and finding underrepresented areas.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I'm really excited about, because it's kind of a loop that closes on itself. One of the things we did for Llama 3 was use Llama 2 to classify the quality of web documents for pre-training. And the first reaction people have is, wait, isn't that circular? You're using the model to decide what the next model learns from? But actually, that's the whole point.

Think about what you have at scale. You have trillions of tokens on the web, and most of it is, frankly, not great. Boilerplate, spam, SEO junk, duplicated content. Historically, people used very simple heuristics or small classifiers, fastText-style models trained on things like Wikipedia versus random Common Crawl. Those are cheap, but they're crude. They can't really tell you whether a document is educational, whether it's well-reasoned, whether it's the kind of text you'd actually want a model to internalize.

With a large language model, you can ask much richer questions. Does this page contain knowledge? Is it written clearly? Would an expert consider this high quality? And Llama is good enough at reading comprehension that its judgments correlate well with what humans would say. So you prompt it, you get labels on a sample, and then you distill that into a smaller, fast classifier you can run over the whole corpus, because obviously you can't run a 70B model on every document on the internet.

What I find valuable is that it moves the bottleneck. Instead of being limited by what a tiny classifier can perceive, you're limited by how well you can articulate what good data looks like. And that's a much more interesting problem. You can target domains. You can say, I want more math, more code, more reasoning-heavy text, and the model can recognize those even when they're not obviously labeled.

And then there's the flywheel aspect. Each generation gets better at understanding text, so it gets better at curating data, which makes the next generation better. That's a very different dynamic than just scraping more and hoping scale fixes everything. Data quality is honestly one of the biggest levers we have left, maybe bigger than architecture at this point, and having a model smart enough to help you with it is a huge deal.

r001.rationale: The response says Llama can recognize targeted domains such as math, code, and reasoning-heavy text, but does not explain that generated topic tags are used to adjust the pre-training mixture or balance topical diversity.

astra-6.text:
What I find valuable is that you can turn a very broad question—“Is this useful training data?”—into something much more specific. You can ask Llama to classify the topic, assess whether a page is educational, or identify the kind of reasoning it contains. That gives you a richer signal than just filtering on surface properties of the text.

Then you can use those signals to build different data mixtures and test what actually improves the model. The classifier’s judgment isn’t the final answer; the pre-training experiment is. But it gives you a practical way to explore the data at scale, without having humans read every page.

r001.rationale: The response says Llama can classify topics and that the signals can be used to build different data mixtures, but it does not say the mixtures are adjusted to balance topical diversity.

sol-6.1.text:
What’s valuable is that you can use Llama to curate the data for the next model. The web is incredibly heterogeneous, and a simple heuristic doesn’t necessarily tell you whether a page contains useful information. With a language model, you can ask more nuanced questions: Is this educational? What topic does it cover? Is it the kind of content we want in the training mix?

Then you can use those classifications to select and balance the data. And that creates an interesting feedback loop: a better model helps you identify better data, which helps you train a better model.

r001.rationale: The response says Llama can classify what topics pages cover, then use those classifications to select and balance the data in the training mix.
